newsitem.title: USA: Intel seeks summary judgment in DEC suit.
newsitem.headline: Intel seeks summary judgment in DEC suit.

text.p: Intel Corp. Tuesday asked a judge to rule on its breach-of-contract lawsuit against Digital Equipment Corp. without a jury trial.

Intel, the world's biggest computer chip maker, also restated in its motion -- filed in U.S. District Court in San Jose, Calif. -- that it does not have to supply Digital with Pentium computer chips past the third quarter, when a supply contract between the companies runs out.

Santa Clara, Calif.-based Intel is suing Digital to force the computer maker to return confidential documents about Intel products in the works. PC makers such as Digital rely heavily on these documents to plan their own product offerings.
Intel asked for the documents back shortly after May 13, when Digital sued Intel for allegedly infringing on some of its patents on chip technology.

In the motion, Intel said it had a right to ask for its documents back under a contract between the companies. Because "there can be no dispute about the material fact," Intel wants the judge to rule on the case without a jury, the motion said.
Digital, based in Maynard, Mass., said Intel's request was a diversion.

"Intel's filing of a partial summary judgment motion is another attempt to divert attention from the real issue between the parties -- Intel's infringement of Digital's patent," Digital spokesman Dan Kaferle said.
"We will answer the motion in due course, although it is hard to understand why it was filed. Our view is that the motion is a purely diversionary tactic," he said.
Digital sells many more Intel chips than its own high-speed Alpha chips. Kaferle said Digital "has strictly observed confidentiality terms under which these documents were provided."
Intel also said in the motion that it does not have an obligation to supply Digital with Pentium chips beyond the third quarter when the purchase order runs out.
"Intel is no more obligated to continue to provide DEC with Intel confidential information than it is obligated to continue to provide DEC with Intel processors," Intel said.
Digital executives have said they have a "long-standing" supply agreement with Intel, which would prevent Intel from cutting off the supply.
